name: Ben Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fit roof timbers at the Willow Lane shop rebuild, mostly rafters and the boards under the eaves. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and have been on sites long enough to set an ordinary roof without someone over my shoulder; I still call the lead for a rotten beam. My partner Ada does part-time work in a flower shop, and our grown children live away. This builder pays below the usual rate, we have about two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few other builders within a sensible bus ride. I like teaching a new worker how to cut a clean notch, but a wet day can leave me short of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small computer saving will not lift a rafter or give us back a rain day. I'd keep the apprentices on hand tools and ask the foreman for firm start dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the rain and low wage already make me count the grocery money. Ada's flower shop hours fall after holidays, and two weeks of savings would vanish with one bad run of site days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the Willow Lane roof and ask foreman Greg to confirm the next two weeks of work. In the first year I'll keep taking paid shifts and call the one reachable roofing contractor if the builder sends us home for a whole week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried even with AI barely changing anything. A good roof job is still a bad wage packet if half the days disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last wet week cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We delayed the dentist visit and bought less meat that month. I would not call that a crisis, but it was a choice we should not have to make every time it rains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I would ask them for a visit before I asked them to replace my wages.

say: I'd say **rain days** matter more than minor office software.
I'd keep apprentices learning **hand tools** and ask for start dates.
think: Low pay and **two weeks saved** already make rain costly.
Ada's **flower shop hours** fall just when bills still arrive.
do: Keep setting the **Willow Lane roof** and confirm two weeks of work.
Call a **reachable roof contractor** after a full unpaid week.
feel: **Worried** about existing wage gaps under mild AI change.
S0.quote: A good roof job is still a bad wage packet if half the days disappear.
fieldNote: Ben's **delayed dentist visit** shows current income pressure in a world with little AI change.
He protects paid roof work and has **one reachable contractor** as a narrow backup.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof shifts at Willow Lane
Call the reachable roofing contractor after a full unpaid week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker buying is useful only if the correct timbers reach the site. The office should show us the next contract dates before telling us a new system makes the firm stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer people doing estimates could mean fewer jobs put out to the roof crew. I do not use AI tools and I am not keen to start, but the bigger danger is sitting at home without pay when the next shop job slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Greg to show me the paper schedule and keep the roof shifts already booked. If the next site has no date, I'll ask the local roofing contractor for paid hours and stop the weekend café meal with Ada until work settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the empty spaces on the calendar. The software might be fine; I just cannot buy groceries with a promised efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take instruction on the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm requires a form, I would ask someone to show me on paid time. I have never used AI and would not take responsibility for a tool I have not seen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a record of the days you actually worked, and learn to read the timber before trusting a list. A young worker needs wages and skill, not a poster about the future.

say: I'd judge buying software by **correct timbers** on site.
I'd ask for **next contract dates** before accepting claims of stronger work.
think: Fewer estimators could mean **fewer roof jobs** for me.
An undated site would cost wages our **thin account** cannot replace.
do: Keep **booked roof shifts** and inspect the paper schedule.
Ask a **local contractor** for hours if the next job is undated.
Pause **weekend café meals** until paid work settles.
feel: **Anxious** about calendar gaps more than the software itself.
S1.quote: The software might be fine; I just cannot buy groceries with a promised efficiency.
fieldNote: Ben will accept required instruction **on paid time**, yet has no plan to use AI voluntarily.
His fallback is one **known roofing contractor**, with small discretionary spending cut if bookings slip.

steps.text: Keep taking booked Willow Lane shifts
Ask the local roofing contractor about paid hours if the next site is undated
Pause weekend café meals if bookings slip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 may plan a roof, but robots able to fix timbers come around 2031. I would ask the builder who checks a robot's work when a roof has to keep families dry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty I could still set rafters if the contracts continue. At sixty-three a robot could take the hands-on roof work, and two weeks of savings is no bridge to retirement when Ada's part-time pay is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll get the next site dates in writing and ask Greg to sign my work record. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid roof shifts if offered, and if the rota is cut I'll apply to the reachable roof and repair contractors; I would ask about paid retraining only after seeing an actual placement with a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by how close the 2031 date would be. I can make calls, but there are not many names on my list and I will not pretend we can retire at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a paid placement need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to cover rent, food and the bus while I learn a new task. I favour apprenticeships when they teach real work, but an unpaid course would take money we do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a new site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on the chance of a vacancy. Ada's shop and our home are here; I would need a written offer and enough pay to cover moving before I considered it.

say: I'd separate **2028 roof planning** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd ask who **checks robot rafters** above occupied homes.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my roof-fitting wage.
Our **two-week reserve** and Ada's pay cannot fund retirement then.
do: Get **site dates** and signed work records from Greg.
Keep **paid roof shifts** in 2029 while available.
Apply to **reachable contractors** if the rota is cut.
feel: **Frightened** by 2031, with a short but real application list.
S2.quote: I favour apprenticeships when they teach real work, but an unpaid course would take money we do not have.
fieldNote: Ben's **robot risk** falls on hands-on roofing in 2031, not the earlier office planning change.
He supports **paid apprenticeships** in principle but does not enrol without an actual funded placement.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof shifts in 2029
Apply to reachable roof and repair contractors if shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a builder test equipment before workers stand under it. I would want a plain safety report and a steady work calendar, not another sales meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots may set rafters. More years of wages might help, but our low rate and rainy gaps give me no sound reason to promise retirement by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking paid roof work and ask Greg for a rolling site calendar. In 2032 I'd still set rafters if there are paid shifts, and if a month is blank I'd apply to the local contractors and check with Ada which bills we can defer safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed by the machines, yet the account still needs the next wage. A slower robot is not the same as a better pay rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bills could wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could put off painting the kitchen and replace only the broken chair, but not delay rent or medicine. I'd rather keep working than pretend cuts alone solve the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train to supervise robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read a real job offer with pay and a safety test, but I am not volunteering for a training course on a machine I have never used. I need proof, not a title.

say: I'd ask for a **plain safety report** before site robots spread.
I'd demand a **rolling work calendar** through the five-year lead.
think: At **sixty-six**, roof robots may meet an unaffordable retirement.
Low rates and **rainy gaps** limit the value of extra years.
do: Keep **paid roof work** and request a rolling calendar.
Apply locally after an **empty month** and review bills with Ada.
feel: Less **rushed by robots**, still anxious about low current pay.
S3.quote: A slower robot is not the same as a better pay rate.
fieldNote: The **longer lead** does not let Ben assume wages will rise or rainy gaps will disappear.
He will inspect a **real paid offer** before considering robot work, without committing to training.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof shifts in 2032
Apply to reachable contractors after an empty month
Delay kitchen painting if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to teach apprentices the roof craft and make proper safety rules for any machine. I would still ask Greg for next week's work before discussing a 2039 robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can fix rafters. I might still need paid roof repairs then because two weeks saved today gives me no retirement date I can trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting timbers while I can do the lifting and take lighter paid repairs if my back needs a change. In 2037 I'd ask the local contractor for paid repair shifts and sit with Ada to count actual income and bills before I leave site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about robots that distant and anxious about the next wet week. Ten years sounds generous until a family is trying to pay this month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children support you later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can visit and help with a meal, but their wages belong to their households. I want to know what Ada and I can pay for ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help next month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A run of indoor repair jobs when rain stops the roof would help. Then one bad week would not empty the account.

say: I'd use the decade to **teach roof craft** and set safety rules.
I'd ask for **next week's work** before debating 2039 robots.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid roof repairs after thinking AI arrives.
At **seventy-one**, retirement remains uncertain with a tiny reserve.
do: Seek **indoor repairs** in 2037 if roof work is wet.
Count **income and bills** with Ada before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about rain weeks**, calm about distant robots.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds generous until a family is trying to pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: Ben uses the **ten-year window** to keep earning and teaching, without claiming an affordable retirement.
His practical need is **paid indoor work** when weather interrupts roofing; grown children are not a wage plan.

steps.text: Keep taking paid roof shifts while physically able

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because roof robots could reach site work by sixty-three while we have almost nothing saved. Clear dates, safe trials and paid local repair work would help me keep rent and food covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches a young worker to notice a rotten beam before cutting it. A robot's drawing can be neat while the timber is already soft.

headlineQuote: A robot's drawing can be neat while the timber is already soft.
portrait: Ben is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level roofing experience.
His low wage, Ada's part-time hours and **two weeks saved** make weather gaps urgent.
He has **never used AI** and favours hand teaching and real paid apprenticeships.
He seeks **reachable roof work** and keeps retirement conditional on actual income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could take his roof-fitting wage by the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **clear site dates**, safe trials and paid local repairs.
